THE GUARD IS A PAIR, ONE PER DIRECTION, AND EITHER ALONE PROVES NOTHING: a `takeReading` that ignored its argument entirely passes every other assertion in that describe block, because the offer is still written, still read back, still null on the second read, and still replaced by a second offer. All of that stays true. WATCHED FAILING: mutating the check to drop only the destination comparison turns exactly those two red and leaves the other 379 green. THE SHAPE WORTH CARRYING is the same family as a-generated-value-with-no-consumer seen from the other end — there one producer and no reader, here one slot and two readers. The question that finds both is "how many things touch this, and does it know?" A mailbox, a cache, a module-level singleton and a route parameter all answer it the same way, and all of them are correct until the second caller arrives.

links.guard: gate:test — asserted PER COMPONENT in a loop over OUTFIT_COMPONENTS with harmony skipped, because "the overall moved" passes for an implementation that moved the wrong one. Watched failing: applying the multiplier to contrast turns exactly that test red.
links.rationale: A HABIT IS EVIDENCE ABOUT TASTE AND NOT ABOUT LEGIBILITY. `scoreOutfit` returns six components and preference feedback (FR-37) multiplies EXACTLY ONE of them — `harmony`, the component about how colours sit together, which is what "repeated selection of a pairing" is evidence about. The other five depend on not being reachable from it: `cvdAccessibility`, because whether two colours separate for a deutan is a fact about vision rather than about what somebody keeps picking; `contrast`, because a legibility floor is not negotiable by habit; `personalFit`, because the profile is what the person SAID about themselves while preference is what they DID, and letting one write the other makes the profile unfalsifiable; `corpusAffinity`, a measured dE00 to a published entry; and `versatility`, a property of the colour rather than of this wardrobe. THE FAILURE THIS PREVENTS, STATED PLAINLY: if preference reached `cvdAccessibility`, somebody who repeatedly chose a pairing a deutan cannot separate would gradually stop being told so — THE PRODUCT WOULD LEARN TO AGREE WITH THEM ABOUT AN ACCESSIBILITY FINDING. That is golden rule 13 defeated from an unexpected direction: not by removing the channel, but by teaching the system to stop using it. The same shape applies to `contrast`; a floor that erodes with use is not a floor. THE BOUND IS PART OF THE SAME GUARANTEE. The multiplier is clamped to plus or minus 25% around exactly 1, which is not tuning — it is what keeps preference NUDGING THE ORDER THE ENGINE PRODUCED rather than overruling it. An unbounded multiplier eventually promotes a pairing the engine scored badly, and at that point the six component scores are decoration: the answer is the person's habit wearing the engine's clothes. FR-11 promises a decomposition a person can argue with, and nobody can argue with a number that is mostly their own past behaviour reflected back. THE GUARD IS PER-COMPONENT, in a loop over OUTFIT_COMPONENTS with `harmony` skipped — NOT a check that the overall moved, because "the overall moved" passes for an implementation that moved the WRONG component, which is the entire failure. Watched failing: applying the multiplier to `contrast` as well turns exactly that one test red and leaves the other 120 green. THE OTHER HALF IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE AND IS ASSERTED SEPARATELY: preference must never reach the PUBLISHED RULE CONTENT, which is immutable at a version with a digest. The mechanism that prevents it is that preference lives in a device table the content pipeline cannot see, and the assertions are that the serialised RuleSet is byte-identical after scoring with a preference and that recording one touches no other table.

links.guard: gate:content (the lexicon parses, is digest-verified, carries a rationale per term) plus gate:test (removing a term removes the gap names that used it, watched failing). NEITHER reaches an editor removing a term nobody is currently missing — see the rationale.
links.rationale: THE PHRASE LEXICON HAS TWO READERS NOW, AND THEY FAIL DIFFERENTLY. Until F-048 `content/rules/phrase-lexicon.*.json` had one consumer — the Finder (F-021), which matches what a person types. F-048's `gaps` added a second, naming a missing region from the same 18 published terms. WHEN AN EDITOR REMOVES A TERM the two break in ways that are not comparable: the Finder stops matching a phrase somebody types, which is visible and self-reporting because they search and get nothing; `gaps` loses the ability to NAME a region, so no gap is reported there — and SILENCE IS EXACTLY WHAT "you have no gaps" LOOKS LIKE. A removed term does not make gap analysis wrong, it makes it QUIETER, and a wardrobe with a real hole reports nothing while nobody types a query that comes back empty. WHY THE VOCABULARY LIVES IN CONTENT ANYWAY: inventing a second one inside coverage.ts would be E-013's shape, one content rule in two places drifting the first time an editor publishes. The lexicon has a rationale per term, a version and a digest; a hard-coded list in the engine has none of those and nobody would notice it diverging. So the trade is deliberate — THE GAPS THIS FEATURE CAN NAME ARE EXACTLY THE ONES THE LEXICON CAN EXPRESS — and it is written into the function's own header rather than left to be deduced from an empty result. THE GUARD AND ITS LIMIT: gate:content verifies the lexicon parses, is digest-verified and carries a rationale per term; gate:test asserts that REMOVING A TERM REMOVES THE GAP NAMES THAT USED IT, which is the decoy proving the words come from content rather than from the file, watched failing by hard-coding two term names and seeing exactly that one test of 139 go red. WHAT NEITHER REACHES is an editor removing a term nobody is currently missing — there is no check saying "this lexicon can still express every region a wardrobe might lack", because that would require knowing every wardrobe. The honest mitigation is that the term count is small and each carries a rationale an editor had to write, so removal is a deliberate act rather than a drift. THE NEAR-NEUTRAL BOUNDARY IS THE SAME NUMBER IN TWO PLACES AND THAT IS CORRECT: `gaps` only names regions below NEUTRAL_CHROMA (0.039) because above it a lightness-and-chroma region has a hue nobody published, and the lexicon's own `neutral` term ends at exactly 0.039. One is a CONTENT boundary an editor chose for a word and the other is an ENGINE boundary F-101 measured for when a hue angle stops meaning anything. They agree today and are free to disagree: if an editor widened `neutral`, `gaps` should still refuse to invent a hue above where the engine says hue is real. MOVED IN F-110: `coverage.ts` and its test now live in `@irodora/optimization`, the package F-048's own row named. Nothing above changes in substance — the reader is the same code at a new address. The "one test of 139" watched failing above was counted when the file was in `recommendation`; those 18 coverage tests are now 18 of 28 in `optimization`, and the decoy is the same decoy.

links.guard: gate:typecheck and gate:build — removing or renaming any of these from the index of @irodora/recommendation is an immediate compile error in @irodora/optimization, naming the file. gate:lint additionally fails on a cycle, which is what the reverse edge would be. NEITHER reaches the WRONG FIX for that compile error, which is the actual hazard — see the rationale.
links.rationale: F-110 moved `coverage.ts` into `@irodora/optimization`, the package F-048 was scoped to. Inside `recommendation` it reached `NEUTRAL_CHROMA`, `OUTFIT_SLOTS`, `scoreOutfit`, `Candidate`, `OutfitComponent`, `OutfitPiece`, `OutfitSlot`, `PersonalProfile` and `RuleSet` as RELATIVE IMPORTS — internal, and freely refactorable by anyone working in that package. Across a package boundary they are PUBLIC API, and nine symbols changed status without changing a line of their own source. THE COMPILE ERROR IS LOUD AND THE WRONG FIX IS SILENT. Removing `NEUTRAL_CHROMA` from recommendation's index while tidying what looks like an internal constant fails typecheck immediately and names `coverage.ts`, so nobody ships that by accident. The hazard is the repair: the cheapest-looking fix is to declare 0.039 locally in `optimization` and move on. That is E-013’s shape — one rule in two places — and it is worse here than usual, because `NEUTRAL_CHROMA` is not a preference. F-101 MEASURED it as the chroma below which a hue angle is a rounding artefact, and `gaps` refuses to name a hue above it for exactly that reason. A second copy would drift from the measurement and nothing would go red. THE DIRECTION IS THE PART TO HOLD: `optimization` imports `recommendation` because a solver optimises over a score, and NEVER the reverse. ARCHITECTURE.md now names this edge rather than leaving it to be inferred, because an unstated rule is the one somebody reverses. A cycle fails lint, so the reverse edge cannot ship — but it can be attempted, and the doc is what says why not to. WHY MEDIUM AND NOT HIGH: every path here fails a gate loudly and immediately. This link exists to make the dependency DISCOVERABLE BEFORE somebody tries, so the repair is "import it" rather than "redeclare it".

links.guard: gate:test — the capsule tests build their fixtures with the SAME join that coverage.ts uses, so a change to the separator or the sort breaks parsing and the brute-force comparison disagrees loudly. NEITHER that nor any type reaches a garment id that CONTAINS the separator, which is the silent case — see the rationale.
links.rationale: F-048 built `Coverage.combinations` as a `ReadonlySet<string>` of sorted, `|`-joined garment ids, and documented it as state `applyChange` needs so an increment is a set operation rather than a guess. THE JOIN WAS AN IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL: `applyChange` only ever compares and subtracts whole keys, so it never has to know what is inside one. F-050 SPLITS THEM. `solveCapsule` reads the set as its problem instance and does `c.split('|')` to recover the garment ids, so a private encoding became a contract between two modules the moment a second reader parsed it. Nothing in the type system says so — both sides see `string`. THE LOUD FAILURE AND THE SILENT ONE. Changing the separator, or dropping the sort, breaks parsing in a way the capsule tests catch immediately, because their fixtures build keys with the same join and the brute-force oracle then disagrees. That is fine. The SILENT failure is a garment id that contains a `|`: the key still parses, into the WRONG NUMBER OF WRONG IDS. The solver would then optimise over garments that do not exist and return a capsule naming them, with an outfit count that is internally consistent and wrong. No gate here can see it. WHY IT IS NOT A LIVE DEFECT TODAY: garment ids are UUIDv7 from `@irodora/store` and slot-index strings in fixtures, and neither can contain a separator. This is recorded because THE CONSTRAINT NOW EXISTS AND IS WRITTEN DOWN NOWHERE ELSE — the day an id becomes user-supplied, or a slug, or anything a person types, this is the link that says why that is not free. THE FIX IF IT EVER BINDS is not to escape the separator, which moves the problem, but to carry the combination as the ids it already is rather than a string that has to be taken apart again. That is a change to F-048s public type and it is deliberately not made here: there is no defect to fix yet, and a type change to satisfy a hypothetical is how a small file becomes a large one.

links.guard: gate:state (the retired-surface check), which since F-107 reads docs/architecture and docs/adr and, since F-107 widened the vocabulary, knows the server-tier words. Proven by scripts/verify-retired-docs-proof.mjs — nine cases, including the superseded filter watched BOTH ways on the same file. THE GUARD DOES NOT COVER THE SOURCE. `.harness/rules` is NOT in the scan corpus (F-112), so the file at the FROM end of this link is the one place the check cannot see. That is the gap, and it is stated rather than implied.
links.rationale: A RULES FILE IS NOT A DESCRIPTION, IT IS A SOURCE. Somebody planning a feature reads .harness/rules/security/security.md and writes acceptance criteria from it, so a false sentence in a rule does not stay in that file — it is COPIED, in good faith, into the scope of work that has not been done yet. THIS IS EVIDENCED, NOT HYPOTHESISED. security.md said "decoding happens only in the worker, never in the API process" nine months after ADR-0051 removed both. F-042 was planned from it and its criterion 4 read "EXIF stripped on ingest; images decoded only in the worker under hard limits" — a criterion that could not be satisfied by anything anyone could build, in a feature that shipped. What shipped decodes on the device under a byte cap and a header-read pixel cap, which is the criterion s intent; the criterion itself was corrected by F-107 rather than marked, because it did not name the worker to forbid it, it ASKED for it. THE MOMENT THE VOCABULARY WIDENED, THE CHECK FOUND IT. F-107 added the server-tier terms and gate 0 immediately flagged F-042.acceptance[3] — a criterion in the scope file, which was always in the corpus, in words the corpus did not know. That is the whole shape of this link in one observation: the check was looking in the right place for the wrong words. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR ANY RULE CHANGE: a rule that stops being true does not merely become stale prose. It becomes a supply of plausible, unbuildable requirements, and the features planned from it carry the error past every gate — because a criterion is a string, and a well-formed string describing a system that does not exist is exactly what the retired-surface check exists for and exactly what it cannot see without the vocabulary. THE DIRECTION IS ONE-WAY AND WORTH SAYING: criteria are written from rules, never the reverse. Correcting a criterion does not correct the rule it came from, so a fix at the TO end leaves the source intact to be copied again.

links.guard: gate:test — the screen suite recomputes the expected weight with preferenceWeight itself and compares, so a screen carrying its own formula fails (watched: replacing the call with accepted/(accepted+rejected) failed exactly that test and nothing else). gate:typecheck catches the signature. NEITHER REACHES THE PROSE. `preferences.formula` explains the curve in words, in two locales, and no check ties that sentence to the constant it describes — see the rationale.
links.rationale: preferenceWeight HAD ONE CALLER, inside the engine, where the number fed a ranking and nobody saw it. F-109 added a second with a different need: the screen renders the number AND THE INPUTS IT CAME FROM, because FR-37 says a person can SEE their preference weights. WHAT CHANGES ABOUT CHANGING THE FORMULA. Before, altering the curve changed a ranking — observable only as different recommendations, and defensible as tuning. Now it changes a number a person is looking at beside the counts it is derived from. F-046 chose "linear to saturation, then flat" over a sigmoid FOR THIS EXACT REASON, and said so: "each of the first eight nets moves it one eighth of the way" is a sentence somebody can check by hand. That property is only worth anything once there is a screen, and now there is one. THE SCREEN NEVER RECOMPUTES. It imports preferenceWeight rather than reimplementing the curve, and the test recomputes the expected value with the same function instead of asserting literals — so a private copy in the app fails rather than agreeing today and drifting later (E-008s shape, applied to a formula rather than to colour maths). THE GAP THE GUARD DOES NOT COVER: the screen also renders PREFERENCE_SATURATION and a sentence explaining what it means, in English and Japanese. Change the constant and the number on screen follows automatically; change the SHAPE of the curve and the sentence becomes false while every test stays green, because no check ties prose to the behaviour it describes. That is the same class as the claims lint and it is not solved here.

links.guard: gate:artefact (16, at a tag) + script:verify-manifest-permissions.mjs (the config half, on every pull request)
links.rationale: ADDING A DEPENDENCY CAN ADD AN ANDROID PERMISSION, and neither the import nor app.config.ts will mention it. Two mechanisms, both silent: a package ships its own android/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml which the MANIFEST MERGER folds in by design, and a package ships an Expo CONFIG PLUGIN which Expo autolinks and which can call withPermissions itself. THIS HAS NOW HAPPENED TWICE. expo-file-system declares INTERNET, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE and WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE in its own manifest, and it is not even a direct dependency — it arrives transitively and is autolinked. F-043 then added expo-image-picker, whose plugin does `if (microphonePermission !== false) withPermissions([RECORD_AUDIO])` — OPT-OUT, for callers who capture video. This app passes mediaTypes: [images] and records no audio anywhere, and the microphone permission reached a signed artefact. THE FIX IS AT THE SOURCE, NEVER THE EXPECTATION. Adding RECORD_AUDIO to EXPECTED_PERMISSIONS would have turned the gate green and shipped a microphone permission on a colour tool — the precise outcome the gate exists to prevent, reached by editing the thing that objected. The plugin is now listed with microphonePermission: false (the only way to pass it an option, since Expo autolinks it either way) AND the permission is in blockedPermissions, because plugin options are the kind of thing a refactor drops. WHAT TO DO WHEN ADDING A NATIVE DEPENDENCY: read its android manifest and its app.plugin.js before merging, and expect the permission list to be a property of the BUILT FILE rather than of any file you wrote. That is why gate 16 reads the artefact — every other check in this repository looks at source, and source is exactly where this class is invisible. F-114 CLOSED THE CONFIG-PLUGIN HALF OF THE DELAY AND NOT THE OTHER HALF. verify-manifest-permissions.mjs reads the manifest expo prebuild writes, on every pull request after gate 6, and asserts the KEPT permissions equal EXPECTED_PERMISSIONS minus the three that arrive at Gradle time — so a plugin that adds one fails the pull request that adds it. USE_BIOMETRIC, USE_FINGERPRINT and DYNAMIC_RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED_PERMISSION remain visible only in the built artefact, the check names all three on every run including a green one, and gate 16 is unchanged. Two checks, two questions: what the config contributes, and what the merger produces.

links.guard: NONE THAT RUNS HERE, and that is the finding rather than an omission. Jest has ONE runtime and no worklet boundary, so a function missing the directive is an ordinary function that the existing lens tests call directly and pass. Typecheck sees a normal call; lint sees an import that resolves. The only thing that can catch this is a device — F-040s first attestation, which is still OUTSTANDING. F-116 files the static check that would close it.
links.rationale: THE LENS CRASHED ON ITS FIRST FRAME AND THE CAUSE WAS THREE WORDS. `sampleFrame` runs on VisionCamera's frame-processor thread and carries `'worklet'`. It called `sampleStride` from `camera.ts`, which carried nothing. A worklet may only call other worklets: the Worklets babel plugin captures an unmarked import as an ordinary JS-thread function, and invoking it from the frame thread throws the moment a frame arrives — which is the moment the Lens opens. THE DIRECTIVE IS A PROPERTY OF THE CALLEE, NOT OF THE CALL SITE. Marking `sampleFrame` says nothing about what `sampleFrame` may reach. Every function reachable from a worklet has to declare itself one, in its own source, and a caller being correct is not evidence about its callees. IT IS STILL AN ORDINARY FUNCTION EVERYWHERE ELSE, which is why the existing tests passed before the fix and pass after it. That symmetry is exactly what makes the defect invisible: nothing about the JS-thread behaviour changes, so no JS-thread test can distinguish the two states. WHAT WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN. F-040 attested "VisionCamera frame processors run on a worklet thread and the UI thread never blocks on colour maths" and that attestation is OUTSTANDING — gate 0 has printed it on every run since F-040 closed. The feature shipped with the one claim that would have caught this explicitly unproven, and the first person to open the Lens found it. An outstanding attestation is not paperwork; it is a list of the things nobody has run. THE WHOLE SURFACE IS SMALL AND IS NOW ENUMERATED: three worklets exist in this repository — `onFrame` and `sampleFrame` in viewfinder.tsx, `sampleStride` in camera.ts — and after this change every function they reach is marked. `readCaptureSpace` is deliberately NOT marked: it is called from `onSessionConfigSelected`, on the JS thread.

links.guard: NONE THAT RUNS HERE, and saying so is the point. Jest has one runtime, no worklet boundary and no camera, so neither delivery path executes in any test — the viewfinder is the reason `Lens` takes a node instead of building one. Typecheck sees a boolean ref; lint sees a ref that is read and written. The failure mode is a Lens that still shows A reading, so even a device check has to look at whether the colour CHANGES when the camera moves, not whether one appeared. F-040s first attestation — frame processors run on a worklet thread — is still OUTSTANDING and remains the only thing that could cover this.
links.rationale: THE LENS NOW HAS TWO DELIVERY PATHS AND ONLY ONE FLAG SEPARATES THEM. `scheduleOnRN` pushes a sample from the frame runtime to the JS thread; a `Synchronizable` written BEFORE that push is polled at 4 Hz as a fallback, because F-120 showed the frame worklet running 51 times while nothing arrived. `pushed` is what switches the fallback off, and it is set ONLY inside `deliver` and `report` — the two callbacks `scheduleOnRN` invokes. SET IT FROM THE POLL AND THE LENS FREEZES ON ONE FRAME. The first polled reading would mark the push as working, the interval would early-return forever after, and the screen would hold a single colour that never updates. That is a WORSE failure than the one being fixed, because it looks like success: a reading is on screen, with provenance, at the right confidence. Nothing about it says it is two seconds stale, and nothing about it says it is the same two seconds an hour later. IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT `seenFrame`, and the two are one line apart. `seenFrame` answers "has anything at all arrived", which the 2-second timer needs and which the POLL is entitled to set. `pushed` answers "did the push mechanism work", which only the push can answer. Collapsing them is the obvious simplification and it is the bug. THE ORDER INSIDE THE POLL IS PART OF THE SAME CONTRACT. If `scheduleOnRN` is what fails, every frame writes BOTH a good sample and a thrown message, so reading `thrown` before `latest` would cover a working viewfinder with an error about a mechanism nobody is using. The throw is reported only when nothing was sampled and nothing was refused. WHY THE FALLBACK IS NOT SIMPLY THE DESIGN: 4 Hz against NFR-4s 50 ms live-pick budget. It is a path that keeps the Lens usable while the device tells us which of the two candidates it is. Promoting it would be a decision, and decisions take an ADR.

A PRICE IS STORED AT A SCALE THE ROW DOES NOT RECORD. `garment.cost_minor` is an INTEGER of minor units and `garment.currency` is a three-letter code; NOTHING on the row says how many minor units the code has. The exponent comes from this table at WRITE time (costEntry) and from the same table again at READ time (formatMinor). While the two agree, every price round-trips exactly. CHANGE ONE ENTRY AND EVERY PRICE ALREADY WRITTEN FOR THAT CURRENCY IS SILENTLY REINTERPRETED. Adding a currency at exponent 0 that was previously falling through to the ISO default of 2 divides every stored price for it by a hundred on the way out; removing one multiplies by a hundred. There is no compiler error, no failed read and no exception — a garment simply reports a different cost per wear than it did yesterday, in the plausible direction, and the person looking at it has no way to tell. It is the E-001 shape applied to money: a value derived at write time that nothing recomputes on read. WHY THE TABLE IS NOT SIMPLY MOVED ONTO THE ROW. A `minor_unit_digits` column would make each price self-describing and it would be the right answer if prices were ever exchanged between devices or between versions of this table. They are not yet — there is one local database, one writer, and no import path for a price — so the column would be storage for a problem that does not exist, and F-042 refused exactly that shape twice (no digest column, no image_path). WHAT THE GUARD CAN AND CANNOT DO. `cost.test.ts` pins EVERY non-default entry by value — all twenty-six — plus the ISO default, so an edit to this table cannot land quietly: the suite goes red and names the currency. A test over a handful of examples would have let a change to CLP or IQD through, which is why it is exhaustive rather than illustrative. That makes the change VISIBLE, which is all a test can do — it cannot migrate data that is already on somebody's phone. If an exponent here is ever corrected, the correction is a migration question before it is an edit, and this link is the record that says so.

THE ENGINE EMITS MESSAGE KEYS AND HOLDS NO CATALOGUE, WHICH IS RIGHT AND WHICH LEAVES ONE END UNCHECKED. `scoreColor` returns a `FactorContribution.messageKey` and `scoreOutfit` returns component keys; rendering them is the app's job (FR-11, ADR-0056), because a sentence produced in the engine would have to be translated at scoring time and a stored recommendation would become a stored English string. The cost is that `messageKey` is a plain `string` on the engine's side of the boundary and a `MessageKey` only on the app's, so THE ENGINE CAN NAME A KEY THE CATALOGUE DOES NOT HAVE with typecheck green — and the app renders a blank line, or whatever `t()` does with a key it has never seen. E-016 is the reverse direction (en is the source of the key set and ja must match it) and cannot see this at all. IT WAS NOT A THEORETICAL GAP. Until F-052 NOTHING IN THE APP CALLED scoreColor: all twelve of its `explain.<factor>.<direction>` keys had been emitted since R3 and none had ever been in either catalogue. FR-29 asks for a per-factor explanation and the engine had been producing one for two releases into a catalogue that could not name it. The gap was invisible rather than absent, which is why the first consumer is where it had to be found. THE GUARD PINS THE SET IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES IT SAFE TO EXCLUDE THESE KEYS FROM THE UNUSED-KEY SCAN. `i18n.test.ts` asserts (a) every key `MESSAGE_KEYS` can produce exists in `en`, and (b) every `explain.*` key in `en` is one the engine emits. The second matters because these are rendered through a COMPUTED lookup — `t(f.messageKey)` — so no source literal exists and the existing 'has no key nobody renders' scan, which is a source-literal scan, cannot see the consumer. Without (b) the exclusion would open exactly the placeholder hole that scan exists to close. Both directions were proven by mutation: deleting `explain.chroma.neutral` failed (a) and (b); adding an `explain.sparkle.supports` the engine never emits failed (b) and three more. THE OUTFIT-COMPONENT KEYS ARE A DECLARED GAP, NOT AN EXCLUSION. `OUTFIT_MESSAGE_KEYS` have no catalogue entries — `OutfitBuilder` renders the raw component name beside each score — and the test asserts the missing set EXACTLY, so the existing gap stays visible and attributable while a NEW unrenderable key still fails. Filtering them out would have made the test quietly stop covering them. THE SCREEN NARROWS RATHER THAN CASTS. `t(key as MessageKey)` would compile and render nothing; `Shopping.tsx` checks membership and falls back to the raw key, so a miss is visible and reportable instead of blank. This guard is what stops that fallback ever being reached.

links.guard: gate:lint — scripts/verify-android-min-sdk.mjs, seven cases with the decoys watched failing. The ones that matter are the LOWERED values: 24 and 25 are both rejected, because a check that only noticed a MISSING number would pass the edit that actually happens — somebody widening device support. Two more reject a plugin that hard-codes the number instead of passing the constant, INCLUDING when the literal is 26, because two numbers that can disagree is the shape this regresses in. The real config must stay green. WHAT THE GUARD CANNOT DO: prove the built APK declares it. That is the artefact gate s job, where aapt2 is an independent oracle, and it runs only in CI.
links.rationale: A NUMBER IN A CONFIG FILE DECIDES WHICH BRANCH OF A DEPENDENCY S C++ EXISTS. react-native-nitro-modules guards its entire AHardwareBuffer implementation behind `#if __ANDROID_API__ >= 26`, with a `throw std::runtime_error` in the `#else`. __ANDROID_API__ is set by the NDK toolchain from Gradle s minSdkVersion, and Nitro takes the app s value directly: `minSdkVersion getExtOrIntegerDefault("minSdkVersion")`. This repository never set one, Expo s ProjectConfiguration.kt falls back to `warnIfNotDefined("minSdkVersion", 24)`, and so the `#else` is what shipped. THE GUARD AND THE CALL DISAGREED, AND THAT IS THE PART TO REMEMBER. Frame.hasPixelBuffer returned TRUE the whole time, because it asks the same question with only the RUNTIME half: `if (SDK_INT >= P) hardwareBuffer?.use { if (it.isCpuReadable) return true }`. One is a property of the DEVICE; the other is a property of OUR BUILD. No runtime check on the JavaScript side could ever have bridged that, which is why the try/catch F-121 put around getPixelBuffer() is what turned an invisible throw into a sentence — after four device round trips. IT IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY OTHER CHECK HERE. Jest has no NDK. Typecheck sees an integer. Lint sees a plugin entry that resolves. The failure appears only on a phone, on every frame, inside react-native-vision-camera-worklets own try/catch, as a console.error — which is to say nowhere a person holding the phone can read. WHY IT LIVES IN app.config.ts AND NOWHERE ELSE: apps/mobile/android/ is generated and untracked, and both android-build.yml and release.yml run `expo prebuild --platform android --clean`. A value written into the generated project by hand works locally and vanishes on the next run, which is how a fix becomes a mystery a fortnight later. WHY 26 AND NOT 28: 26 is the number in the #if. A device on API 26 or 27 never reaches the HardwareBuffer path at all — it falls to the single-plane branch, which works at any level — so a higher floor would drop two API levels and buy nothing. WHAT IT COSTS: Android 7.0 and 7.1 can no longer install the app. That cost is close to zero because the app ALREADY did not work there — reading a colour is a core journey and it threw on every frame — and because NFR-7 sets the bar at a four-year-old mid-range Android, which in 2026 means API 31 or above. Declaring 24 was a claim the binary could not honour.
